raw_case_text:
The third N. cerradoensis strain was isolated from the sputum sample of an 82-year-old man with pulmonary emphysema. On October 16, 2014, the man sought care in the study hospital's emergency department for increasing dyspnea of a few days' duration that had not improved despite treatment with corticosteroids and levofloxacin (500 mg 1x/d for 3 days). The patient had frequent coughing with yellowish expectoration but no fever; he received a diagnosis of respiratory infection and alteration (worsening) of his COPD status. Thoracic scan results showed cylindrical bronchiectasis and subpleural consolidations in both lungs; culture of a sputum sample obtained on October 22 was positive for N. cerradoensis and Aspergillus fumigatus. Because of the patient's clinical status, the A. fumigatus was considered a colonizer (i.e., present without causing active disease). He was hospitalized and given trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (160/800 mg 2x/d for 30 days) for treatment of the N. cerradoensis infection. Cultures of sputum samples collected on December 3 and 16 were negative for Nocardia species.
The 3 N. cerradoensis isolates showed the same antimicrobial susceptibility pattern: nonsusceptibility to amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, minocycline, and ciprofloxacin (MICs >64/32 mug/mL, >4 mug/mL, and >8 mug/mL respectively) and susceptibility to ceftriaxone, imipenem, linezolid, amikacin, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (MICs <8 mug/mL, <0.25 mug/mL, 1 mug/mL, <0.25 mug/mL, and <0.5/9.5 mug/mL, respectively). After XbaI digestion, isolates from the first 2 patients had indistinguishable PFGE patterns that differed from that of the third patient's isolate (Figure). However, no epidemiologic relationship could be established between the first and second patients: they lived in different villages ( 50 km apart) and had not been hospitalized nor been in the hospital's outpatient clinic or emergency department at the same time.
Because of the environmental origin of Nocardia species, their isolation, particularly in respiratory samples, might indicate colonization rather than clinical infection. In these cases, N. cerradoensis was isolated from the bronchial secretions of 3 patients who were at high risk for development of Nocardia clinical infection because they were immunosuppressed as a consequence of long-term corticosteroid therapy for COPD. The first and third patients received a diagnosis of pulmonary nocardiosis and were specifically treated with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, with symptom resolution. However, the physicians in charge considered the presence of N. cerradoensis in the second patient to be a colonization rather than active disease. This diagnosis was reinforced by the quick disappearance of the pathogen from respiratory samples without specific treatment (the patient received only a short course of amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, to which N. cerradoensis was resistant).

subjective.chief_complaint: An 82-year-old man with pulmonary emphysema presented with a few days of worsening dyspnea and frequent cough productive of yellowish sputum.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: On October 16, 2014, the patient presented to the emergency department with several days of worsening shortness of breath and frequent productive cough with yellowish expectoration without fever, unresponsive to 3 days of outpatient corticosteroids and oral levofloxacin (500 mg once daily).
subjective.past_medical_history: Pulmonary emphysema/COPD maintained on long-term corticosteroid therapy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for fever; recent outpatient levofloxacin 500 mg daily for 3 days and corticosteroids.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile with clinical signs of COPD exacerbation.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic CT scan demonstrated bilateral cylindrical bronchiectasis and subpleural consolidations. Broth microdilution susceptibility testing of the sputum Nocardia cerradoensis isolate showed susceptibility to ceftriaxone (MIC <8 ug/mL), imipenem (<0.25 ug/mL), linezolid (1 ug/mL), amikacin (<0.25 ug/mL), and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (<0.5/9.5 ug/mL), and nonsusceptibility to amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (>64/32 ug/mL), minocycline (>4 ug/mL), and ciprofloxacin (>8 ug/mL).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Pulmonary nocardiosis caused by Nocardia cerradoensis (with concomitant Aspergillus fumigatus considered an airway colonizer) in a corticosteroid-treated COPD patient was confirmed via sputum culture collected on October 22, 2014, and molecular/PFGE characterization. Hospitalization and targeted treatment with oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (160/800 mg twice daily for 30 days) resulted in complete symptom resolution and negative follow-up sputum cultures on December 3 and December 16, 2014.
